title: SHE SHARED HIS BED… BUT DID SHE EVER HAVE THE RIGHTS OF A WIFE?
paragraphs: SHE SHARED HIS BED… BUT DID SHE EVER HAVE THE RIGHTS OF A WIFE?

The disturbing truth about wives and concubines in ancient Israel—and how the women living in the shadows of Scripture reveal the difference between what human beings permitted, what God intended, and the grace Jesus came to bring.
Imagine being a woman who belongs to a household but never truly feels secure in it.

You share a man's bed. You may bear his children. You may spend years raising a family, preparing meals, enduring pregnancies, and carrying responsibilities that look remarkably similar to those of a wife.
But when decisions are made about your future, your security, or your children, you discover something painful.
You do not necessarily have the same standing as the woman called his wife.
And perhaps the most unsettling part?
The Bible speaks about women who lived in precisely these kinds of arrangements.
Abraham had Sarah—and Hagar.
Jacob had Leah and Rachel—and Bilhah and Zilpah.
David had wives and concubines.
Solomon's household became so enormous that Scripture records seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines.

And somewhere in the book of Judges, there is a woman whose suffering is so horrifying that her story should make every reader stop and ask whether we have confused something the Bible records with something God approves.
So here is the question we must face.
What was the real difference between a wife and a concubine in ancient Israel?
Was a concubine simply another wife?
Was she a mistress?
Was she a slave?
Did God approve of this arrangement?
And if marriage was supposed to reflect covenant faithfulness, why did some of the most prominent men in Scripture have concubines?
The answer is more complicated than many sermons admit.
And what we discover may change not only how we read the Old Testament, but how we understand the difference between human power and God's original design.
Because before we can understand the woman living in the shadows, we must first understand the world that placed her there.

In ancient Israel, marriage was not merely a private romantic commitment. It was also a recognized social and family relationship involving household membership, kinship, economic responsibilities, inheritance, and the continuation of a family line.
A wife generally occupied a recognized marital position within that household, although her rights and security varied according to her circumstances and the historical period.
A concubine, by contrast, was a woman in an ongoing, socially recognized sexual and domestic relationship with a man, but usually with a subordinate status compared with a principal wife.
That distinction matters.
The Hebrew word commonly translated concubine is פִּילֶגֶשׁ (pîlegeš).
The word appears in passages such as Genesis 35:22, Judges 19:1, and 2 Samuel 5:13.
Its precise etymology remains uncertain. What matters is how the biblical narratives use it.
A pîlegeš was not necessarily a secret lover or a woman involved in an illicit affair. She could belong openly to a man's household and be recognized as his partner.
Yet her standing was generally lower than that of a principal wife.
The Hebrew word אִשָּׁה (ʾiššâ) can mean either woman or wife, depending on the context.
This helps explain something that can initially seem confusing.
In Judges 19, the woman identified as a concubine is also described through marital language. Her male partner is called her husband, and her father is described as his father-in-law (Judges 19:3–4).
In other words, a concubine was not always outside the category of marriage in the way a modern reader might assume.
She could be understood as a secondary wife.
But secondary did not mean equal.
And this is where the historical distinction becomes painfully human.

A principal wife generally had a more established position within the household. A concubine could have recognized domestic and marital standing while possessing less social authority, weaker security, or more limited claims in matters involving inheritance and family succession.

There was no single, uniform rule governing every concubine in every biblical period. Some were enslaved women. Others occupied different dependent positions. The status of their children also varied.
We must resist the temptation to impose one modern legal definition on every ancient household.
Still, the recurring pattern is unmistakable.
A concubine could be recognized as a man's partner without enjoying the same position as his principal wife.
And the consequences were not merely theoretical.
They affected real women.
Real children.
Real families.
Real suffering.
Consider Hagar.
Her story begins in Genesis 16, and it is one of the most emotionally complicated accounts in the patriarchal narratives.
God had promised Abram descendants.
Years passed.
Sarai remained childless.
And the waiting became unbearable.
Genesis 16:2 records Sarai's proposal that Abram have a child through her Egyptian servant Hagar.
The Hebrew narrative then says that Sarai gave Hagar to Abram לְאִשָּׁה (ləʾiššâ)—meaning as a wife (Genesis 16:3).
That detail is important.
Hagar was not simply described as an anonymous sexual partner.
The text uses marital language.
Yet Hagar was also Sarai's enslaved servant, and she did not enter the arrangement with the same freedom, authority, or standing as Sarai.
The biblical account does not tell us that Hagar freely chose this arrangement.
We should not pretend that it does.
Imagine the vulnerability.
A woman taken from Egypt.
Living in another family's household.
Placed into a reproductive arrangement designed to solve someone else's anguish.
Then, when she conceives, the relationship between the women deteriorates.
Sarai treats her harshly.
Hagar runs away.
And suddenly the woman whose body had become part of a household's plan is alone in the wilderness.
But here is the detail I do not want you to miss.
God sees her.
Genesis 16:13 records Hagar's response to the Lord who had spoken to her:
אַתָּה אֵל רֳאִי
ʾAttâ ʾēl roʾî.
Commonly translated, “You are the God who sees me.”
The Hebrew expression has interpretive complexity, but its central significance in the narrative is unmistakable: Hagar recognizes that she has been seen by God.
Not merely by Abram.
Not merely by Sarai.
Not merely as a servant.
Not merely as the woman carrying a child.
God sees Hagar herself.
And later, when Hagar and Ishmael are sent away, Genesis 21 records God's concern for them in the wilderness.
This does not mean every human action in their story receives divine approval.
It means God's attention reaches people whose vulnerability is easily overlooked.
There is a difference.
A profound difference.
And perhaps someone reading this knows what it feels like to be useful to others but invisible as a person.
To be needed without being cherished.
To be included when someone wants something from you and forgotten when your own heart begins to break.
Hagar's story does not promise that every painful situation will resolve the way we want.
But it refuses to let us believe that social status determines whether God sees a human being.
The household may have called her a servant. Scripture lets us hear her speak about the God who saw her.
And that is not the end of the story.
Because the next generation exposes another difficult reality.
Jacob loved Rachel.
But he married Leah first through Laban's deception.
He later married Rachel.
Then both sisters gave their servants, Bilhah and Zilpah, to Jacob in connection with their struggles over childbearing.
Genesis 30 describes these arrangements.
Genesis 30:4 uses the expression ləʾiššâ, “as a wife,” when Rachel gives Bilhah to Jacob.
Yet Genesis 35:22 identifies Bilhah as Jacob's concubine.
And Genesis 35:25–26 recognizes the sons born through Bilhah and Zilpah among Jacob's children.
Pause there.
The sons of these women became part of the ancestral story of Israel.
Their mothers occupied subordinate positions, but their children were not simply erased from the family.
This reveals why it is inaccurate to claim that the children of concubines could never inherit or never be recognized.
The biblical evidence is more complicated.

Sometimes a woman's status affected her children's standing. Sometimes those children were recognized as heirs or members of the lineage. Household decisions, paternal recognition, and particular historical circumstances mattered.
Even within Genesis, the experiences of Ishmael and the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah are not identical.
The Bible gives us stories, not one universal legal formula.
And there is something else here.
These arrangements did not eliminate jealousy.
They did not guarantee emotional security.
They did not create a household free from rivalry.
Instead, the narratives of Abraham and Jacob reveal households marked by longing, favoritism, competition, conflict, and grief.
The people involved were not fictional symbols.
They were human beings living with the consequences of human decisions.
And Scripture is honest enough to let those consequences remain visible.
Now we need to confront an important question.
If God did not originally design marriage around concubinage, why does the Old Testament contain laws and narratives involving these arrangements?
Because biblical description and divine prescription are not the same thing.
The fact that Scripture records an action does not mean Scripture commands it.
The fact that a patriarch practiced something does not mean every aspect of his behavior is a model for believers.
Abraham's faith is commended in Scripture.
That does not make every decision Abraham made morally exemplary.
David is remembered as a significant king in Israel's history.
That does not mean his treatment of women was always righteous.
Solomon received extraordinary wisdom.
That does not mean his marital arrangements represented God's ideal.
In fact, Scripture explicitly warns Israel's kings against multiplying wives.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says that the king must not multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away.
And 1 Kings 11:1–4 presents Solomon's many marriages as contributing to his spiritual downfall.
Solomon's seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines are not presented as evidence of extraordinary holiness.
They become part of a warning.
The man famous for wisdom did not consistently live according to the wisdom he had received.
What a sobering reminder.
You can possess knowledge of God and still make decisions that draw your heart away from Him.
You can be surrounded by abundance and still be spiritually impoverished.
You can have a thousand relationships and still fail to honor covenant faithfulness.
And this leads us to the laws themselves.
Exodus 21:7–11 addresses a female servant in an ancient household arrangement involving marriage or betrothal.
The passage places obligations upon the man and provides certain protections for the woman.
Exodus 21:10 is particularly important because it states that if the man takes another wife, he must not diminish the first woman's food, clothing, or marital rights.
The Hebrew text includes the words:
שְׁאֵרָהּ כְּסוּתָהּ וְעֹנָתָהּ
šəʾērāh, kəsûtāh, wəʿōnātāh.
These are commonly understood as provisions relating to food or sustenance, clothing, and marital or conjugal rights.
The final term has generated discussion among interpreters, but the traditional understanding concerns the obligations owed within the marital relationship.
This passage is sometimes connected to the study of concubinage because it concerns a woman of dependent status in a marital arrangement.
However, we must be precise.
Exodus 21:7–11 does not explicitly use the Hebrew word pîlegeš.
It should not be presented as though it were a complete legal code defining every concubine's rights.
What it does demonstrate is that the Mosaic law addressed vulnerable women within existing social structures and imposed obligations upon men who might otherwise exploit their position.
That distinction is essential.
A law regulating an existing institution does not necessarily establish that institution as God's original ideal.
Jesus Himself gives us a principle for understanding this tension.
When questioned about divorce in Matthew 19, Jesus directs His listeners back to creation.
He acknowledges that Moses permitted divorce because of the hardness of human hearts.
Then He says:
“But from the beginning it was not so.” (Matthew 19:8, KJV)
Those words are not a direct statement about concubinage.
We should not pretend that they are.
But they reveal how Jesus distinguishes between accommodations made within a fallen human society and God's original purpose.
And when Jesus explains marriage, He does not point to Solomon's palace.
He points to Genesis.
To the beginning.
To God's design.
Genesis 2:24 says that a man shall leave his father and mother, hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.
The Hebrew expression is:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד
bāśār ʾeḥād.
“One flesh.”
Jesus quotes this foundational passage in Matthew 19:4–6.
And He concludes that what God has joined together, human beings must not separate.
The creation account presents marriage as a profound union, not a hierarchy of women competing for different levels of recognition.
This does not mean every difficult question about ancient marriage disappears.
It means that Christians must allow Jesus to shape their understanding of marriage rather than treating every patriarchal household arrangement as a command to imitate.
And if we want to understand why that matters, we must enter one of the darkest chapters in the Bible.
Judges 19.
There is no responsible way to discuss concubines in ancient Israel without acknowledging this woman.
The narrative tells of a Levite and his concubine.
After a separation, the Levite travels to her father's home, and the two eventually depart together.
They arrive in Gibeah.
What follows is an account of devastating sexual violence.
The woman is handed over to a mob.
She is abused through the night.
By morning, she is found collapsed at the doorway.
The Levite's subsequent actions and the events that follow are horrifying.
Her suffering becomes part of a larger national crisis.
And throughout this terrible account, the woman is never given a personal name.
We should not turn her suffering into entertainment.
We should not romanticize the man who failed her.
We should not mistake the brutality recorded in the chapter for an example of God's approval.
Judges repeatedly exposes the moral disorder of Israel during that period.
The book's concluding assessment is devastating:
“Every man did that which was right in his own eyes.” (Judges 21:25, KJV)
Judges 19 is not a celebration of concubinage.
It is part of a narrative exposing a society in profound moral collapse.
And the woman's story forces us to confront something that remains relevant.
A religious identity does not automatically produce righteous behavior.
The man in this story was a Levite.
He was associated with a tribe entrusted with religious responsibilities.
Yet his position did not guarantee that he would protect the vulnerable woman in his care.
That should trouble us.
Because sometimes people know the language of religion while failing to demonstrate the character of God.
Sometimes the people who should offer protection become part of the danger.
And sometimes those who have been harmed are told to remain silent because the truth might embarrass a household, a leader, or a community.
But Scripture does not erase this woman's suffering.
It preserves the account in all its horror.
Not to invite us to stare at her pain.
But to make it impossible for us to pretend that everything done among God's people reflects God's heart.
A person can carry a religious title and still betray the responsibility to love.
That truth should humble every one of us.
And it should especially humble anyone entrusted with spiritual leadership.
Now consider another revealing passage.
In 2 Samuel 12:8, the prophet Nathan confronts David after his sin involving Bathsheba and Uriah.
Nathan speaks of God giving David his master's house and wives.
Some readers interpret this as divine endorsement of polygamy.
But the statement appears within a prophetic confrontation using the language of royal succession and transferred kingship.
It does not establish that every royal marital arrangement represented God's creation ideal.
Nor should we ignore the broader biblical warnings about multiplying wives, the destructive consequences within David's household, or Jesus' teaching about marriage.
Responsible interpretation requires us to read individual verses within the larger witness of Scripture.
The Bible is not asking us to admire every exercise of royal power.
It is exposing what happens when even powerful, privileged people refuse to submit their desires to God.
And now we come to a distinction that is often misunderstood.
Was a concubine the same as a modern mistress?
Not exactly.
A mistress today usually refers to a woman involved in a sexual relationship outside an existing marriage, often secretly or without recognized marital status.
An ancient Israelite concubine could occupy an openly recognized household position.
Her relationship could be understood as a secondary marital union.
That does not make the arrangement equal, fair, or ideal.
It simply means that modern categories do not map perfectly onto ancient social institutions.
Was a concubine always enslaved?
No.
Some concubines were enslaved or dependent servants, as the stories of Hagar, Bilhah, and Zilpah illustrate.
But the Hebrew term itself does not automatically prove that every woman described as a concubine was enslaved.
Was a concubine always childless or excluded from inheritance?
No.
Genesis records sons born to concubines who became recognized members of their father's lineage.
Genesis 25:5–6 also describes Abraham giving gifts to the sons of his concubines while giving his principal inheritance to Isaac.
This illustrates a distinction in succession, but it should not be turned into a universal rule governing every household.
Was a concubine merely a prostitute?
No.
The biblical category refers to an ongoing household or marital relationship, not simply a commercial sexual transaction.
And was a concubine equal in standing to a principal wife?
Generally, no.
That subordinate standing is the central distinction.
The reality was not simply about whether a man had sexual access to a woman.
It was about how the household recognized her, what obligations existed toward her, what security she possessed, and how her position compared with that of another wife.
That is the historical answer.
But if we stop there, we miss the deeper question the Gospel invites us to ask.
What does Jesus reveal about the value of a woman in a world where social rank could determine how she was treated?
Consider the woman at the well in John 4.
Jesus meets a Samaritan woman.
He speaks with her publicly.
He asks her for water.
He engages her in a serious theological conversation.
And He reveals extraordinary truths about worship and His identity as Messiah.
During their conversation, Jesus tells her that she has had five husbands and that the man she now has is not her husband.
John 4:18 records His words:
“He whom thou now hast is not thy husband.” (KJV)
The Greek expression is:
οὐκ ἔστιν σου ἀνήρ
ouk estin sou anēr.
In context, it means that the man she presently has is not her husband.
The Greek word anēr can mean man or husband, depending on context.
Now, we must be careful.
John does not identify this woman as a concubine.
We should not invent that detail.
Nor does the passage tell us why she had five husbands. We cannot responsibly assume that every previous relationship ended because of her personal sin.
She may have experienced circumstances the text does not explain.
What Scripture does tell us is that Jesus knew her situation.
And He did not refuse to speak with her.
He did not treat her as unworthy of hearing the truth.
He did not reduce her entire identity to her relationship history.
He spoke to her about living water.
He confronted the reality of her present relationship without abandoning the conversation.
And He revealed Himself to her.
The woman then went back to her town and invited others to come and see Him.
John 4:39 says that many Samaritans believed because of her testimony.
Think about that.
A woman whose personal history Jesus knew became a witness who directed others toward Him.
She did not need to conceal her story for Jesus to speak truth to her.
And Jesus did not need to pretend that every relationship was a marriage in order to offer her living water.
There is grace here.
Not grace that denies truth.
Grace that brings truth close enough to heal.
This is where the story becomes personal.
Because perhaps you have never been a concubine.
Perhaps you have never lived in an ancient household.
But you know what it feels like to be treated as less important than someone else.
Perhaps you have been in a relationship where you gave everything and received almost nothing.
Perhaps you have been abandoned.
Perhaps someone made promises that were never fulfilled.
Perhaps your past contains decisions you regret, relationships you cannot undo, or wounds you still struggle to explain.
Or perhaps you have been the one who used another person's love carelessly.
Perhaps you have demanded loyalty while refusing responsibility.
Perhaps you have called something love when, deep down, you knew selfishness was driving your choices.
The Gospel speaks to both sides.
To the wounded, Christ offers mercy, truth, and hope.
To the guilty, Christ calls for repentance and offers forgiveness.
To the proud, He calls for humility.
To the broken, He offers Himself.
And to all of us, He declares that our deepest need is not simply a better social position.
It is reconciliation with God.
That reconciliation comes through Jesus Christ.
Not through moral superiority.
Not through religious performance.
Not through pretending we have never failed.
Through the crucified and risen Savior.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were still sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired every mistake.
Not after we learned how to make our lives look acceptable to everyone watching.
Christ died for sinners.
And His resurrection announces that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
The Gospel does not say that every wounded person is automatically innocent of every wrong.
Nor does it say that repentance is unnecessary.
It tells us that forgiveness is possible because Jesus bore our sins, and new life is possible because He rose again.
That is why grace is not permission to continue exploiting people.
Grace teaches us to turn away from sin.
Titus 2:11–12 connects God's saving grace with the rejection of ungodliness and the pursuit of godly living.
Real grace transforms.
It changes how we treat our spouses.
How we speak to women.
How we honor men.
How we protect children.
How we exercise authority.
How we respond to the vulnerable.
And how we take responsibility when we have done wrong.
A man cannot appeal to Abraham's household to excuse selfishness while ignoring Christ's command to love.
A husband cannot point to Solomon's concubines while refusing the sacrificial standard of Ephesians 5:25:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” (KJV)
That is not permission to dominate.
That is a call to costly, self-giving love.
And a woman who has been mistreated does not have to interpret her suffering as proof that God values her less.
The Bible's record of unequal social arrangements does not establish unequal human worth.
Genesis 1:27 teaches that humanity, male and female, is created in God's image.
And Galatians 3:28 declares that believers are one in Christ Jesus.
That verse concerns their unity and standing in Christ; it does not erase every distinction in human relationships or automatically settle every question of social structure.
But it does proclaim something essential.
No believer enters God's family through superior social status.
No woman needs the title of a principal wife to possess the dignity of someone made in God's image.
No man possesses greater access to salvation because he holds authority over others.
At the foot of the cross, none of us can purchase our standing before God.
We come through Christ.
And that brings us back to the question that began this journey.
What was the real difference between a wife and a concubine in ancient Israel?
A wife generally occupied a more established marital position in the household.
A concubine was a recognized but subordinate partner, often understood as a secondary wife, whose rights, security, and social standing could be more limited.
The exact circumstances varied.
Some concubines were enslaved.
Some bore children who were recognized as heirs.
Some lived within royal households.
And some biblical accounts reveal the devastating vulnerability that could accompany their position.
But the difference between a wife and a concubine was not a difference in the amount of God's image either woman possessed.
Social rank could distinguish their positions. It could not determine their human worth.
And perhaps that is one of the most important truths we can carry away from these difficult passages.
The Bible does not conceal the failures of its prominent figures.
It does not pretend every patriarch was a perfect husband.
It does not hide the consequences of rivalry, exploitation, or the abuse of power.
Instead, across the unfolding story of Scripture, it directs our attention toward the One who fulfills God's purposes perfectly.
Jesus Christ.
The faithful Bridegroom.
The One who does not exploit His bride but gives Himself for her.
Revelation 19:7 celebrates the marriage of the Lamb, and Ephesians 5:25–27 portrays Christ's sacrificial love for the church.
This is not a claim that every ancient concubine directly symbolizes the church.
It is a contrast worth contemplating.
Where human relationships are often marked by selfishness, Christ demonstrates self-giving love.
Where human promises fail, Christ remains faithful.
Where sin produces shame and destruction, Christ offers forgiveness and redemption.
And where the world is tempted to measure people by status, wealth, usefulness, or reputation, the Gospel calls us to see them in the light of God's truth.
Maybe this article has made you uncomfortable.
Good questions often do.
But do not leave with only outrage at the past.
Ask what these Scriptures expose in the present.
Do we protect people who depend on us?
Do we honor commitments?
Do we mistake power for righteousness?
Do we use biblical stories to justify what Jesus calls us to surrender?
Do we notice those who suffer quietly inside respectable-looking homes?
And when we have sinned, are we willing to repent rather than hide behind religious language?
The truth is that every one of us needs grace.
Not a sentimental grace that excuses everything.
The costly grace of the Savior who died for our sins and rose again.
If you have never surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, you can turn to Him today.
Confess your sin.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
Ask Him for mercy.
Begin following Him in repentance and faith.
And if you already belong to Christ but have been drifting, return to Him.
You do not need to defend the sin that is destroying your peace.
Bring it into the light.
He is worthy of your trust.
And if this article has touched something deeply personal, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
You do not have to disclose painful details to strangers to prove your faith.
But your honest words may remind someone else that they are not the only person still learning how to trust God.
Someone may need to hear that redemption is possible.
Not because every story ends neatly.
But because Jesus Christ is alive.
If this message helped you understand Scripture more faithfully, please save it. These are passages worth returning to, studying carefully, and discussing with humility.
Not merely to increase a number on a screen, but because someone among your friends may be wrestling with the same questions about the Bible, marriage, suffering, and God's character.
Because we need more than inspirational phrases.
We need the Word of God handled faithfully.
We need the courage to examine difficult passages.
And above all, we need Jesus.
Think of it as an opportunity for regular, voluntary Christian giving—an offering of support for the work of sharing biblical teaching and discipleship resources.
We are saved by grace through faith in Christ, not by financial contributions.
And yet voluntary generosity matters.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not come from compulsion, but from a willing heart.
These products are simply resources and expressions of encouragement. They are not substitutes for Scripture, the local church, or a living relationship with Jesus Christ.
The library is part of our desire to make Christian learning and spiritual nourishment accessible.
Read.
Pray.
Use the free resources.
Continue growing in Christ.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your worth before God.
The mission is not to build a community of people who can afford to pay.
It is to help point people to the Savior who has already paid the price we could never pay for ourselves.
And before you leave, return for a moment to Hagar.
A woman in the wilderness.
A woman whose circumstances were shaped by the decisions of others.
A woman who knew what it meant to live beneath another person's authority.
Yet her story contains one of the most moving declarations in Genesis.
“You are the God who sees me.”

The same Scriptures that record the social divisions of the ancient world also testify to a God who sees the vulnerable, confronts sin, keeps His promises, and ultimately reveals His saving grace through Jesus Christ.
That is the hope we must never lose.
The Gospel does not rewrite history by pretending the suffering never happened.
It changes the future of those who turn to Christ by offering forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and the promise of new creation.
The scars of human failure are real.
The call to repentance is real.
And the mercy of Jesus Christ is real.
So remember this when the world tries to convince you that your past, your position, or another person's treatment of you is the final definition of your life.
You may have been treated as an afterthought in someone else's story, but you were never invisible to the God who gave His Son to redeem sinners.
